This subsection from the article discusses the clinical application prospects of altretamine and cisplatin as therapeutic agents targeting ferroptosis, highlighting considerations in patients with renal or hepatic impairment and the implications of drug metabolism on treatment efficacy.

The potential of altretamine to induce ferroptosis through GPX4 inhibition warrants careful consideration in patients with underlying renal or hepatic impairment, where altered drug metabolism may enhance toxicity or where pre-existing oxidative stress could be exacerbated ( Table 1 ). Cisplatin (DDP) is a well-established chemotherapeutic agent widely used in the treatment of various solid tumors, including bladder, ovarian, and gastric cancers. Its primary anti-tumor mechanism involves forming DNA adducts, thereby interfering with DNA replication and transcription and ultimately triggering cell death. However, in many cases, DNA damage alone is insufficient to elicit robust cell death responses, as cancer cells can adapt by downregulating pro-death pathways and upregulating survival signals [254–256] . One of the key cytotoxic effects of cisplatin is the induction of ROS overproduction, which can damage various cellular components and contribute to its anti-tumor efficacy. Elevated ROS levels may also enhance intracellular iron accumulation, potentially sensitizing cells to ferroptosis. Interestingly, in cisplatin-resistant osteosarcoma cells, levels of ROS, lipid peroxides, and malondialdehyde (MDA) were significantly reduced compared to sensitive counterparts. This resistance is likely linked to the upregulation of antioxidant defense mechanisms, including increased expression of GPX4, a crucial enzyme in suppressing lipid peroxidation and ferroptotic cell death [257–259] . Cisplatin elevates Nrf2 via STAT3 activation, and the resultant STAT3–Nrf2 axis fortifies antioxidant defences in cisplatin-resistant osteosarcoma cells. MG63/DDP and Saos-2/DDP cells exhibit higher p-STAT3, Nrf2 and GPX4 than their parental counterparts, and STAT3 inhibition by BP-1–102 markedly lowers Nrf2 and GPX4, restoring cisplatin sensitivity through elevated ROS, lipid peroxides and MDA [260] . System Xc⁻ modulation dictates ferroptosis induction, apoptosis suppression and cisplatin resistance of head-and-neck cancer cells. Nrf2, restrained by Keap1-mediated ubiquitination, governs iron homeostasis, disabling the Nrf2–ARE axis sensitises resistant HNC cells to artesunate-induced ferroptosis [261] . Low-dose cisplatin transiently arrests ferroptosis in resistant osteosarcoma cells, yet ferroptosis inducers reactivate death pathways, and their combination with cisplatin overcomes resistance [260] . In gastric cancer, cisplatin and paclitaxel trigger CAF-derived miR-522, which suppresses Arachidonic acid 15-lipoxygenase (ALOX15), curbs lipid ROS and fosters drug resistance [262] . Hence, ferroptosis induction reverses this chemoresistance. ATF3 counteracts cisplatin resistance in gastric cancer by repressing Nrf2, Keap1 and System Xc⁻, thereby promoting ferroptosis [263] . The activation patterns of the Nrf2 and System Xc⁻ signaling pathways induced by cisplatin vary across different NSCLC cell lines. Importantly, the extent of this activation correlates strongly with the level of cisplatin resistance observed in these cells. Notably, both pathways are markedly upregulated in cisplatin-resistant NSCLC cells. Within NSCLC cell lines, cisplatin treatment triggers both apoptotic and ferroptotic cell death mechanisms. In the cytoplasm, cisplatin binds GSH, forming a Pt-GS complex. In the cytoplasm, cisplatin drugs bind GSH to form a Pt-GS complex structure. In the cytoplasm, cisplatin reacts with GSH to form Pt–GS complexes, leading to GSH depletion and reduced GPX4 activity, thereby inducing lipid peroxidation and ferroptosis, effects that mirror those elicited by erastin [264] . Subsequent studies have shown that GPX4 inhibitors can partially restore ferroptosis sensitivity in several drug-tolerant cancer models, suggesting their potential as an adjunct target in strategies to overcome therapeutic resistance [265] . Nevertheless, multi-drug combinations carry inherent toxicity risks. Elevating GPX4 inhibitor concentrations markedly enhances oxidative stress sensitivity in drug-resistant cancer cells while extending the therapeutic vulnerability window. This extended timeframe enables completion of targeted therapies or conventional chemotherapy. Implementing temporally staggered treatment regimens may therefore offer significant clinical advantages by maximizing therapeutic efficacy against resistant tumors while mitigating potential toxicities. Consequently, GPX4 inhibitors may effectively potentiate platinum-based drugs against therapy-resistant malignancies [266] . Considering that cisplatin is known for its notable nephrotoxic and neurotoxic effects, the combination with ferroptosis-inducing agents demands heightened vigilance, especially in patients who already have renal dysfunction or neurodegenerative diseases. The induction of ferroptosis, which involves iron-dependent lipid peroxidation and the generation of ROS can significantly increase oxidative stress. In patients with pre-existing renal impairment, this heightened oxidative stress could further damage nephrons, accelerating renal function decline. Similarly, in those with neurodegenerative conditions, the additional oxidative burden could exacerbate neuronal damage and expedite neurodegenerative processes. Therefore, the potential for accelerated functional decline in these vulnerable patient populations necessitates a thorough evaluation of the risks and benefits before proceeding with such combination therapies ( Table 1 ).

This clinical application prospects section from "Targeting ferroptosis in cancer therapy" discusses the selective toxicity of artesunate toward cancer cells and highlights the caution needed in patients with G6PD deficiency, alongside the introduction of gemcitabine as a therapeutic agent.

While artesunate shows promising selective toxicity toward cancer cells, its potent pro-oxidant mechanism necessitates careful monitoring in patients with glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency or chronic hemolytic conditions, where oxidative stress could precipitate hemolytic anemia ( Table 1 ). Gemcitabine (GCB) is a pyrimidine nucleoside analog that is phosphorylated by deoxycytidine kinase (DCK) after being internalized via nucleoside transporters. This phosphorylation leads to the formation of gemcitabine triphosphate (dFdCTP), which is incorporated into replicating DNA, thereby inhibiting DNA synthesis and inducing cell death [2] . Upon entry into the human body, GCB is metabolized into several active forms, all of which have potent inhibitory effects on DNA replication. Despite its efficacy in treating various cancers, the clinical utility of gemcitabine is frequently limited by the development of drug resistance [272–275] .The activity of gemcitabine is regulated by multiple enzymes, and resistance is influenced by complex metabolic and signaling pathways. In PDAC, gemcitabine remains a cornerstone of chemotherapy. Intriguingly, transcriptomic analyses of PDAC tumor samples have revealed a strong association between gemcitabine and ferroptosis inducers. For instance, elevated GPX4 levels have been observed in gemcitabine-resistant PDAC cells. Mechanistically, activation of activating transcription factor 4 (ATF4) upregulates HSPA5, which binds to GPX4, stabilizing it and preventing lipid peroxidation, thereby contributing to ferroptosis resistance [276–278] .Additionally, the sensitivity of PDAC cells to ferroptosis correlates positively with immune-related factors, including high CD8 + T cell infiltration and type II interferon responses. Furthermore, carbonyl reductase 1 (CBR1) plays a protective role against oxidative stress in PDAC cells. Its suppression leads to elevated ROS levels and reduced cell proliferation. Inhibition of CBR1 sensitizes cancer cells to gemcitabine. Notably, flavonoid-albumin conjugates have been shown to bind directly to CBR1, reducing its enzymatic activity, increasing intracellular free iron, inducing ferroptosis, and ultimately enhancing gemcitabine sensitivity [279] . The theory that iron-induced oxidative stress inherently promotes oxidative damage may theoretically exacerbate the toxicity of gemcitabine. However, particular caution is warranted in patients with impaired bone marrow function or preexisting pulmonary disease, as additional ROS-mediated oxidative injury may amplify gemcitabine-induced bone marrow suppression and pulmonary injury .

We also explore various strategies to enhance ferroptosis sensitivity in cancer cells, including the manipulation of cell therapy, transcription factors, regulatory genes, ion homeostasis, organelle functions, and the extracellular environment. Additionally, we examine current and emerging therapeutic agents targeting ferroptosis, discussing their clinical potential and prospects for integration into cancer treatment regimens. By reviewing both the underlying mechanisms and therapeutic approaches related to ferroptosis, this article aims to provide valuable insights into how targeting this unique form of cell death may help address tumor resistance and improve patient outcomes.

Despite its promise, ferroptosis-based therapy faces several critical challenges. First, the development of potent, selective, and bioavailable ferroptosis inducers remains limited. This conclusion section from Zhangshuai Dai's article discusses the need for further exploration of lipid transport proteins and the molecular mechanisms by which intracellular iron contributes to the initiation of ferroptosis in cancer therapy.

Furthermore, the role of lipid transport proteins, beyond STARD7, remains largely unexplored and warrants further investigation. Sixth, the initiation mechanisms of ferroptosis and the activation role of intracellular iron remain active areas of inquiry. While ferroptosis typically begins with intracellular Fe²⁺ accumulation, the precise molecular mechanisms by which iron drives ferroptosis are not fully elucidated. Some studies suggest that ferroptosis is initiated via ROS generation and inhibition of lipid antioxidant systems, while others propose that pharmacological or genetic suppression of antioxidant regulators may be sufficient to trigger ferroptosis. Whether these processes are entirely dependent on iron overload, and how iron orchestrates ferroptotic signaling, remain key questions for future research.

The timeline of key discoveries highlights significant advancements in understanding ferroptosis regulation from 2012 to 2022, showcasing the development of multiple pathways and mechanisms contributing to lipid-based cell death. Caption: Timeline of key discoveries and pathways in ferroptosis regulation. Early studies on oxytosis (1989) highlighted a vulnerability related to GSH/ ROS, foreshadowing the concept of ferroptosis. In 2003, erastin-induced cell death was reported to be iron-dependent, leading to the formal definition of ferroptosis in 2012. Subsequent research identified system Xc⁻ inhibition and GPX4 inactivation (2014) as critical drivers of lipid peroxidation and ferroptosis. The role of ACSL4-mediated polyunsaturated fatty acid–phospholipid (PUFA–PL) synthesis (2016) emerged as a pivotal susceptibility pathway. Notably, vitamin K was identified as a potent ferroptosis inhibitor (2022). Collectively, these discoveries have significantly advanced our understanding of lipid-based cell death and its regulation.

Fig. 2: Inhibition of GPX4 by RSL3 induces ferroptosis, while disruption of SLC7A11 by Erastin also leads to ferroptosis, demonstrating their roles as effective inducers. Additionally, the FSP1 pathway maintains redox homeostasis by neutralizing lipid peroxyl radicals, which counters ferroptosis. The figure underscores the importance of both GPX4-dependent and independent mechanisms in safeguarding against ferroptosis in cancer therapy.

Caption: Integrated antioxidant defense systems against ferroptosis: GPX4-dependent and GPX4-independent mechanisms. (A) The canonical cystine/glutamate antiporter System Xc⁻ and GPX4-centered antioxidant axis suppress ferroptosis by eliminating lipid hydroperoxides. System Xc⁻, composed of SLC7A11 and SLC3A2, imports extracellular cystine (CyS₂) in exchange for intracellular glutamate (Glu). Cystine is reduced to cysteine (CyS), a precursor for GSH biosynthesis catalyzed by glutamate-cysteine ligase (GCL) and glutathione synthetase (GSS). GPX4 utilizes GSH to convert phospholipid hydroperoxides (PUFAs-OOH) into nontoxic lipid alcohols (PUFAs-OH) through a catalytic redox cycle involving selenocysteine (Sec), thereby preventing membrane damage. Inhibitors such as Erastin and RSL3 induce ferroptosis by disrupting SLC7A11 or inactivating GPX4, respectively. (B) Three GPX4-independent radical-trapping antioxidant systems counteract ferroptosis by scavenging lipid peroxyl radicals. FSP1, localized to the plasma membrane, reduces CoQ 10 to ubiquinol (CoQ 10 H₂) using NAD(P)H, which neutralizes lipid radicals. In mitochondria, DHODH catalyzes the reduction of CoQ 10 to CoQ 10 H₂ to suppress lipid peroxidation. Additionally, the GCH1–BH 4 pathway protects cells by producing BH 4 , a lipophilic antioxidant that inhibits ferroptosis and facilitates phospholipid remodeling. Together, these systems operate independently of GPX4 and GSH metabolism to maintain redox homeostasis.
